intro: How Vietnamese is pronounced: the six tones, how the letters sound, the word endings, and a key to the symbols in the pronunciations.

sections.heading: About the pronunciations
text: Pronunciations follow the Hanoi (Northern) standard, written as exact (bracketed) IPA. Vietnamese is written in the Latin alphabet (chữ Quốc ngữ), one syllable at a time: a word like gia đình "family" is two written syllables.

Every syllable has a tone, marked on its main vowel, and the tone changes the meaning: ma "ghost", má "cheek", mà "but". In the pronunciations each syllable's tone is drawn as a small colored line above it (see The six tones below). In the Browse table it is written instead as pitch bars after the syllable, from ˥ (high) to ˩ (low).
Vietnamese has no strong word stress, but in words of more than one syllable the last syllable is a little stronger, so it carries the stress mark (ˈ).

Many words differ in the South (Saigon): r, d and gi are said like English y or r instead of z, the hỏi and ngã tones merge, and some everyday words change (heo for lợn "pig"). The notes on those words give the Southern form.

sections.heading: The six tones
sections.text: Each syllable's tone is drawn as a small colored line above it in the pronunciations: the line traces the pitch, high at the top and low at the bottom.

items.note: ngang (level), no mark — mid and flat
huyền (falling), à — low, falling gently, a little breathy
sắc (rising), á — rising sharply, like a surprised "huh?"
hỏi (dipping), ả — falls low, then rises again in careful speech
ngã (broken), ã — rises, broken in the middle by a catch in the throat
nặng (heavy), ạ — short and low, cut off with a glottal stop
long a, as in "father"
short a, cut off quickly
short "uh", as in "but"
open e, as in "bed"
closed e, like "ay" in "say" without the glide
ee, as in "see"
open o, as in "law"
closed o, like "oh" without the glide
long "uh", as in "fur" without the r
oo, as in "food"
like u but with spread, unrounded lips
ee sliding into "uh"
oo sliding into "uh"
ư sliding into "uh"

sections.heading: Consonants at the start of a syllable

items.note: an implosive b, made by pulling air in slightly
an implosive d, the tongue on the gums
all z in Hanoi; in the South d and gi are y, and r is an r
both s in Hanoi; in the South s is closer to "sh"
both like a soft "ch" in Hanoi; in the South tr is like "tr" in "tree"
k without a puff of air; q always comes as qu [kw]
a rough h, as in German "Bach"
a soft g, made with the back of the tongue barely touching
ng as in "singer", but at the start of the syllable
ny, as in "canyon"
f
t with a puff of air, as in "top"
t without a puff of air, as in "stop"
v
a syllable written with a vowel first starts with a glottal stop [ʔ]

sections.heading: Endings
sections.text: Final consonants are not released: the mouth closes but no air bursts out (marked ̚). After o, ô and u, the endings ng and c are said with the lips closed as well.

items.note: unreleased p, t, k
an unreleased k made farther forward; after a it sounds like "-aik"
ng made farther forward; after a it sounds like "-aing"
ng or k with the lips closed at the same time
glides: y and w
